British Museum.extract: The British Museum is a public museum in the Bloomsbury area of London dedicated to human history, art and culture. Its permanent collection numbers some eight million works and is among the largest and most comprehensive in existence. The museum was established in 1753 and first opened to the public in 1759.

Tower of London.extract: The Tower of London is a historic castle on the north bank of the River Thames in central London. It was founded towards the end of 1066 as part of the Norman Conquest. The White Tower, which gives the whole castle its name, was built by William the Conqueror in 1078.

Big Ben.extract: Big Ben is the nickname for the Great Bell of the striking clock at the north end of the Palace of Westminster in London. The name is frequently extended to refer also to the clock and the clock tower. The tower was renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012 to mark the Diamond Jubilee of Elizabeth II.

Tower Bridge.extract: Tower Bridge is a Grade I listed combined bascule and suspension bridge in London, built between 1886 and 1894. The bridge crosses the River Thames close to the Tower of London and has become a recognisable symbol of the city. It is sometimes confused with London Bridge, about half a mile upstream.

Trafalgar Square.extract: Trafalgar Square is a public square in the City of Westminster, Central London, laid out in the early 19th century around the area formerly known as Charing Cross. At its centre stands Nelson's Column, guarded by four lion statues. The square commemorates the Battle of Trafalgar, a British naval victory of 1805.

St Paul's Cathedral.extract: St Paul's Cathedral is an Anglican cathedral in London and the seat of the Bishop of London. The present structure, dating from the late 17th century, was designed in the English Baroque style by Sir Christopher Wren. Its dome, framing the skyline for centuries, is among the highest in the world.

Buckingham Palace.extract: Buckingham Palace is a royal residence in London and the administrative headquarters of the monarch of the United Kingdom. Located in the City of Westminster, the palace is often at the centre of state occasions and royal hospitality. It has served as the official London residence of British sovereigns since 1837.

Westminster Abbey.extract: Westminster Abbey is a large, mainly Gothic abbey church in the City of Westminster, London. It is one of the United Kingdom's most notable religious buildings and the traditional place of coronation and burial for English and British monarchs. The building's origins reach back to the 10th century.

The Shard.extract: The Shard is a 72-storey skyscraper in Southwark, London, that forms part of the London Bridge Quarter development. Standing 309.6 metres high, it is the tallest building in the United Kingdom. The glass-clad pyramidal tower was designed by the architect Renzo Piano and completed in 2012.

London Eye.extract: The London Eye is a cantilevered observation wheel on the South Bank of the River Thames in London. When it opened in 2000 it was the tallest Ferris wheel in the world. The structure is 135 metres tall and the wheel has a diameter of 120 metres.

Tate Modern.extract: Tate Modern is an art gallery in London housing the United Kingdom's national collection of international modern and contemporary art. It is located in the former Bankside Power Station in the Southwark district. The gallery opened in 2000 and is one of the most visited art museums in the world.

National Gallery.extract: The National Gallery is an art museum in Trafalgar Square in the City of Westminster, in central London. Founded in 1824, it houses a collection of more than 2,300 paintings dating from the mid-13th century to 1900. Entry to the main collection is free of charge.

Natural History Museum.extract: The Natural History Museum in London is a museum that exhibits a vast range of specimens from various segments of natural history. It is one of three major museums on Exhibition Road in South Kensington. The museum is home to life and earth science specimens comprising some 80 million items.

Victoria and Albert Museum.extract: The Victoria and Albert Museum in London is the world's largest museum of applied arts, decorative arts and design. Housing a permanent collection of over 2.27 million objects, it was founded in 1852 and named after Queen Victoria and Prince Albert. It is located in the South Kensington district.

Science Museum.extract: The Science Museum is a major museum on Exhibition Road in South Kensington, London. It was founded in 1857 and today is one of the city's major tourist attractions. The museum holds a collection of over 300,000 items, including many famous artefacts from the history of science and technology.

Hyde Park.extract: Hyde Park is a Grade I-listed major park in the City of Westminster, London. It is the largest of four Royal Parks that form a chain from the entrance of Kensington Palace through Kensington Gardens and on to St James's Park. The park is divided by the Serpentine and the Long Water lakes.

Kensington Palace.extract: Kensington Palace is a royal residence set in Kensington Gardens, in the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea in London. It has been a residence of the British royal family since the 17th century. The palace has been the London home of several senior members of the royal family.

Piccadilly Circus.extract: Piccadilly Circus is a road junction and public space in London's West End in the City of Westminster. It was built in 1819 to connect Regent Street with Piccadilly. The junction is known for its video display and neon signs mounted on the corner building, as well as the Shaftesbury Memorial Fountain.

Covent Garden.extract: Covent Garden is a district in London, on the eastern fringes of the West End. It is associated with the former fruit-and-vegetable market in the central square, now a popular shopping and tourist site. The area is also home to the Royal Opera House, itself known as Covent Garden.

Leicester Square.extract: Leicester Square is a pedestrianised square in the West End of London. It was laid out in 1670 and is today associated with the cinema and film premieres. A number of major cinemas surround the central garden, at the centre of which stands a statue of William Shakespeare.

St James's Park.extract: St James's Park is a 23-hectare park in the City of Westminster, central London. The park lies at the southernmost tip of the St James's area and is the most easterly of a near-continuous chain of Royal Parks. It is bounded by Buckingham Palace to the west and Horse Guards to the east.

Regent's Park.extract: Regent's Park is one of the Royal Parks of London, occupying an area in the north-west part of central London. The park contains Regent's University London and the London Zoo, and is home to an open-air theatre and extensive gardens. It was designed by the architect John Nash.

Camden Market.extract: Camden Market is a name for several adjoining retail markets near Camden Town in the London Borough of Camden. Products sold there include crafts, clothing, bric-a-brac, and fast food. The markets grew from a single craft fair established in 1974 and are among the most visited attractions in London.

British Library.extract: The British Library is the national library of the United Kingdom and one of the largest libraries in the world. Located on Euston Road in London, it holds well over 150 million items in most known languages. The library receives a copy of every publication produced in the United Kingdom and Ireland.

King's Cross Station.extract: King's Cross railway station is a major London railway terminus on the northern edge of central London. Opened in 1852, it serves the East Coast Main Line to the north of England and Scotland. The station is well known for the fictional platform nine and three-quarters from the Harry Potter stories.

St Pancras Renaissance Hotel.extract: The St Pancras Renaissance London Hotel is a Victorian building in London at St Pancras railway station. Designed by George Gilbert Scott in the Gothic Revival style, it opened in 1873 as the Midland Grand Hotel. After decades of decline and closure it was restored and reopened as a luxury hotel in 2011.

Somerset House.extract: Somerset House is a large Neoclassical complex situated on the south side of the Strand in central London, overlooking the River Thames. The site was formerly occupied by a Tudor palace. The present building was designed by Sir William Chambers in 1776 and is today a major arts and cultural centre.

Royal Albert Hall.extract: The Royal Albert Hall is a concert hall on the northern edge of South Kensington, London. Since its opening by Queen Victoria in 1871 the hall has hosted many of the world's leading artists. It is the venue for the annual Proms concerts, which have been held there every summer since 1941.

Marble Arch.extract: Marble Arch is a 19th-century white marble-faced triumphal arch in London. Designed by John Nash in 1827, it was intended to be the state entrance to the courtyard of Buckingham Palace. It now stands on a large traffic island at the junction of Oxford Street, Park Lane and Edgware Road.

Green Park.extract: Green Park, officially the Green Park, is one of the Royal Parks of London. It lies between Hyde Park and St James's Park, and together with these two and the gardens of Buckingham Palace it forms an almost continuous stretch of open land. It is mainly a mature landscape of trees over grass.

Sky Garden.extract: The Sky Garden is a public garden atop the skyscraper at 20 Fenchurch Street in the City of London. Spread across three storeys near the top of the building, it offers landscaped gardens and observation decks with panoramic views over the capital. Access is free but usually requires booking in advance.

Monument to the Great Fire of London.extract: The Monument to the Great Fire of London, known simply as the Monument, is a Doric column in the City of London. It stands near the northern end of London Bridge and commemorates the Great Fire of London of 1666. Designed by Christopher Wren and Robert Hooke, it is 62 metres tall.

Shakespeare's Globe.extract: Shakespeare's Globe is a reconstruction of the Globe Theatre, an Elizabethan playhouse associated with William Shakespeare, in the London Borough of Southwark. The reconstruction was founded by the actor and director Sam Wanamaker and opened in 1997, about 230 metres from the site of the original theatre.

Borough Market.extract: Borough Market is a wholesale and retail market hall in Southwark, London. It is one of the largest and oldest food markets in the city, with a market on the site dating back to at least the 12th century. The present buildings were built in the 1850s and it now specialises in speciality foods.

Trinity Square Gardens.extract: Trinity Square Gardens is a public garden on Tower Hill in the City of London, close to the Tower of London. The gardens contain the Tower Hill Memorial commemorating merchant seafarers and fishermen. The site was historically used as a place of public execution for prisoners held at the Tower.
